newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo banks asked to help make monetary policy work.
newsitem.headline: Yugo banks asked to help make monetary policy work.

text.p: Yugoslavia's economy performed below official forecasts in the first half of 1997, prompting bankers and analysts to question on Tuesday the efficiency of the central bank's monetary policy.
Analysts said the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) had its hands tied after being burdened with the task of ensuring price and currency stability in an inadequate financial and economic environment.

"The monetary authority is facing a dilemma. Is this monetary concept valid or not? If changes are needed, it should be made clear what instruments the NBY has to control the money supply without disturbing the dinar fixed rate," NBY Board of Governors member Djordje Djukic told a bankers meeting.
Djukic said there was a big discrepancy between monetary policy and the overall economy.

"Monetary policy is heading one way but the economy is moving in the opposite direction. Monetary policy did not result in a more intensive industry growth. And an extreme growth in wages means most funds end up in personal income."
Djukic called on bankers to help the NBY make its monetary policy more efficient for the economy.

"We are in a funny situation. Banks do not want to extend credits any longer because they fear they would not be repaid. On the other hand, any changes in the existing monetary instruments or further monetary relaxation threaten to destabilise the dinar exchange rate," Djukic said.
Banks' average daily liquidity exceeded 400 million dinars ($82.5 million) compared to 200 million several months ago. But credit activity was almost non-existent, he said.

Improvement in the bank liquidity followed a sharp monetary expansion since June, when Serbia sold a part of its Telecom stake for nearly $1 billion and after the NBY launched a new 100-dinar banknote.
Despite improved liquidity, banks prefer to keep their lending activity low fearing new credits will never be repaid.
More than 100 Yugoslav banks ended 1996 with 70 million dinar ($12.15 million) losses and 3.5 billion dinars in unrecoverable claims.
Although firms cite expensive bank credits as a major obstacle to higher output, bankers insist commercial lending rates have declined to as low as 3.25 percent.
Banks officially charge 3.25 percent interest on extended credits. The price of bank credits grows with adding various commission fees.
Financial analysts expected bank credit activity to remain low until after presidential and parliamentary elections in Serbia set for September 21.

Analysts saw the latest NBY move to drain surplus liquidity from the banking sector by raising the reserve requirement to 20 from 15 percent as a way to secure funds ahead of August 15 when the state's liabilities towards farmers mature.
Local markets expected no bargaining between the state and the farmers this year, for peasants constituted an important electorate.

Apart from political motives, analysts said the latest reserve requirement increase was a way to prevent any unwanted mounting of inflationary pressures, which traditionally occurs at the end of the summer along with pay-outs to farmers.

Traders said the effects of NBY moves would be short-lived as long as the government refuses to decisively address the problem of burgeoning inter-company debt and provide protection for creditors instead of debtors.
Financial non-discipline has pushed inter-company debt to as high as 8.5 billion dinars in the first half of 1997.
"But that is for politicians to decide. And this is not the right moment for any radical decisions," a trader said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 311 4254 ($ = 4.85 Yugoslav Dinars)
